structure.title: Childhood and education
structure.text: Gateshead and Lowood establish Jane's dependence, resistance, and developing judgments about kindness and authority.

structure.title: Work and belonging
structure.text: Adult settings test how affection, employment, belief, and independence can coexist. Jane narrates these experiences from a later vantage point.

people.name: Jane
people.text: An orphan who becomes a governess.

people.name: Helen Burns
people.text: A school friend with a different response to suffering.

context.title: A governess's position
context.text: A governess is educated to share polite conversation but paid to serve a household. Intimacy and dependence occupy the same rooms.
context.takeaway: Attention does not erase unequal power.

context.title: Different Christian demands
context.text: Characters invoke religion in sharply different ways, from endurance and charity to punishment and duty. Jane must judge these interpretations.
context.takeaway: No single character exhausts the novel's faith.

notice.text: Follow who is permitted to speak frankly.
notice.why: Jane's voice changes the terms on which others recognise her.

notice.text: Notice fire, cold, and enclosed spaces.
notice.why: Physical surroundings make dependence and desire felt before they are explained.

passages.quote: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.

opening: As a child, Jane Eyre thinks she would endure almost anything to be loved. She grows up poor and becomes a governess, accustomed to being useful rather than wanted, until her employer begins seeking her company and enjoying the frankness others have punished. She falls in love with him. When keeping that love would require her to betray her convictions, Jane must face the possibility of being alone again, with very little to live on and every reason to want to stay.
